bib.title: Neural Networks (Chapter 11, The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed.)

question: What are projection pursuit regression and single-hidden-layer neural networks as nonlinear statistical models, how are they fitted and regularised, and how do they perform?

limits: Chapter covers one-hidden-layer 'vanilla' nets with sigmoid units and back-propagation; no ReLU, SGD variants with momentum/Adam, dropout, batch norm or deep nets beyond the 1989 ZIP-code convnets (dated, 2009).
Simulation uses a single training set of 100 cases (authors say typical) and 10 random starts; sample sizes for the Fig 11.4 mixture example are not restated.
ZIP-code results are from Le Cun (1989) on 320 train / 160 test digits; authors note the test data were implicitly used in tuning, so real error is higher.
Only screened-feature results in the NIPS comparison are legitimate; ARD reduced sets come from the Bayesian NN. Authors say random forest strength 'came as a surprise'.
Interpretation is hard (unidentifiable alpha_m), limiting use in medicine; nets 'are not a fully automatic tool'.
practices: Standardise inputs to mean 0, SD 1 so regularisation treats inputs equally and starting weights have a meaningful range (Sec 11.5.3, p.400).
Start with small random weights, uniform on [-0.7, +0.7]; never exact zero (symmetry, zero derivatives) and avoid large weights (Sec 11.5.1, p.397-398, p.400).
Regularise by weight decay (ridge-like penalty, lambda chosen by cross-validation) or early stopping with a validation set (Sec 11.5.2, p.398).
Prefer too many hidden units (5 to 100) with regularisation over cross-validating the unit count (Sec 11.5.4, p.400).
Try several random starts; average predictions of networks, not weights; or bag (Sec 11.5.5, p.400-401).
Fix the least-constrained setting (zero decay, ten hidden units) and cross-validate the other parameter; test error is less sensitive to decay than to units (Sec 11.6, p.402).
For classification use softmax output with cross-entropy, equivalent to linear logistic regression on hidden units (Sec 11.3-11.4, p.393-395).
Use conjugate gradients or variable-metric methods rather than plain back-propagation or Newton (Sec 11.4, p.397).
Online learning needs learning rate decreasing with sum gamma = infinity and sum gamma^2 finite, e.g. 1/r (Sec 11.4, p.397).
Build problem-specific constraints (local connectivity, weight sharing) from subject-matter knowledge (Sec 11.7, p.407).
Choose and test NN software carefully; quality varies and input scaling matters (Sec 11.10, p.414).

terms.definition: f(X) = sum_m g_m(w_m^T X), an additive model in derived features V_m = w_m^T X with unspecified g_m
g_m(w_m^T X), which varies only in the direction defined by w_m
a model class that can approximate any continuous function arbitrarily well as M grows
the M = 1 PPR model, known in econometrics
two-stage regression or classification model: Z_m = sigma(a0m + a_m^T X), T_k = b0k + b_k^T Z, f_k(X) = g_k(T)
g_k(T) = exp(T_k)/sum_l exp(T_l), positive outputs summing to one
units computing derived features Z_m, so called because Z_m is not directly observed
gradient descent via a forward and backward sweep using the chain rule; errors satisfy s_mi = sigma'(a_m^T x_i) sum_k b_km delta_ki
one sweep through the entire training set
penalty R(theta)+lambda*J(theta), J = sum beta^2 + sum alpha^2, analogous to ridge regression
J = sum beta^2/(1+beta^2) + sum alpha^2/(1+alpha^2), shrinks smaller weights more
train only a while, stopping well before the global minimum, shrinking the model toward linear

terms.term: local connectivity / weight sharing / convolutional network
terms.definition: each hidden unit sees a small patch; units in a feature map share the same weights, so networks are sometimes known as convolutional
weights for feature j into the first hidden layer share a prior variance sigma_j^2; features with small posterior variance are discarded
MCMC with an auxiliary momentum vector and Hamiltonian dynamics to avoid random-walk behaviour

problems: Text has ligature characters (fi, ff) so some quotes avoid them; figure plot-point noise in the cache.
Inconsistency: Sec 11.9.1 says the average 'estimates the posterior mean (11.21)' but the predictive integral is Eq 11.20; Eq 11.21 is the generic weighted-average form.
Inconsistency: 11.9.1 says samples from 'the posterior distribution Pr(Ynew|Xnew,Xtr,ytr)' but they sample the parameters theta from Pr(theta|Xtr,ytr).

Inconsistency: Fig 11.11 caption and text say Net-1 to Net-5 are fit with sum of squares and the text says Table 11.1 gives 'optimal test performance', while 11.4 text prefers cross-entropy; not a contradiction but note the ZIP nets are not softmax/cross-entropy.
Weight decay 0.02 for Fig 11.4 appears only in the figure title, not in the text; Fig 11.4 is described as 'the mixture example of Chapter 2' without sample size.
Ex 11.5 data model (sigma + squared term, noise 0.30) differs from the Sec 11.6 models; not an error.
